items.followUp: What is the purpose of the <ol> tag in HTML?

rubric.why: Identifies the purpose of the UL tag.
rubric.description: States that UL creates an unordered or bulleted list.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either description.

rubric.why: Shows how items are placed in the list.
rubric.description: States that each list entry is enclosed in an LI tag.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying LI as the tag for list items.

modelAnswer: The <UL> tag creates an unordered (bulleted) list in HTML.
Each item in the list is written inside an <LI> tag.

items.followUp: Differentiate between text colour and page background colour.

rubric.why: Identifies what foreground colour changes.
rubric.description: Foreground colour is the colour of text or other foreground content.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as the text/content colour.

rubric.why: Identifies what background colour changes.
rubric.description: Background colour is the colour behind the text or content.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying it as the colour behind the content.

modelAnswer: Foreground colour is the colour of the text or other content shown in front.
Background colour is the colour displayed behind the text or content.

items.followUp: Define a flowchart and state two advantages and two disadvantages of using one.

rubric.why: A definition must describe an algorithm as a sequence of steps.
rubric.description: Defines an algorithm as a finite, ordered sequence of steps for solving a problem.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable definition including steps and a problem or task.

rubric.why: Credits the stated benefits of algorithms.
rubric.description: Gives advantages such as being easy to understand or communicate, helping plan a program, or helping detect errors.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving three valid advantages.

rubric.why: Credits the limitations of algorithms.
rubric.description: Gives disadvantages such as taking time to write, becoming difficult for complex problems, or lacking a standard graphical representation.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for three valid disadvantages; award 1 mark for two valid disadvantages.

modelAnswer: An algorithm is a finite, ordered set of unambiguous steps for solving a problem.
Advantages: It is easy to understand; it helps plan a program; it helps find errors in the logic.
Disadvantages: It can take a long time to write; it can become difficult for complex problems; there is no single standard graphical representation.

items.followUp: Define star and ring topologies, and sketch both.

rubric.why: Identifies the defining feature of bus topology.
rubric.description: Defines bus topology as devices connected to one common backbone cable.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the shared backbone description.

rubric.why: Identifies the defining feature of mesh topology.
rubric.description: Defines mesh topology as devices connected to one another, with links between every pair in a full mesh.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the interconnections.

rubric.why: Checks that the bus diagram shows devices attached to a common line.
rubric.description: Draws a bus diagram with a backbone and devices branching from it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a recognisable labelled bus sketch.

rubric.why: Checks that the mesh diagram shows multiple direct links.
rubric.description: Draws a mesh diagram with devices interconnected by direct links.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a recognisable mesh sketch showing interconnections.

modelAnswer: Bus topology: All computers are connected to one common backbone cable.
Bus diagram: PC1 ─┬────────────┬─ PC2
[Backbone cable]
Mesh topology: Each computer is connected directly to the other computers in a full mesh.
Mesh diagram: PC1 ───── PC2
PC3

items.followUp: Name four types of cybercrime and give one example of each.

rubric.why: Credits one correctly identified cybercrime with an example.
rubric.description: Names hacking and gives an example of unauthorized access to a computer or network.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the crime-example pair.

rubric.why: Credits a second correctly identified cybercrime with an example.
rubric.description: Names phishing and gives an example involving a deceptive message or website used to steal information.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the crime-example pair.

rubric.why: Credits a third correctly identified cybercrime with an example.
rubric.description: Names identity theft and gives an example of stolen personal information being misused.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the crime-example pair.

rubric.why: Credits a fourth correctly identified cybercrime with an example.
rubric.description: Names cyberbullying and gives an example of harassment or threats online.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the crime-example pair.

modelAnswer: Hacking: gaining unauthorized access to a computer system, for example breaking into someone’s email account.
Phishing: using a fake email or website to steal information, for example asking a user for their bank password.
Identity theft: stealing and misusing another person’s personal information, for example using their details to make a purchase.
Cyberbullying: harassing or threatening someone online, for example sending repeated insulting messages through social media.

items.followUp: Name four common symbols used in a flowchart.

rubric.why: Credits the main flowchart symbols used for beginning, processing and input/output.
rubric.description: Names terminal, process and input/output symbols.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming at least three of these symbol types.

rubric.why: Credits additional flowchart symbols or connectors.
rubric.description: Names the decision symbol and flow lines or connectors.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming at least two additional valid items.

modelAnswer: Common flowchart requirements are the terminal (Start/Stop), process, input/output, decision, flow-line (arrow), and connector symbols.

items.followUp: Draw a flowchart to find the product of two input values.

rubric.why: Checks that the flowchart adds the two values and stores the result.
rubric.description: Includes the operation SUM = A + B.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct addition operation.

rubric.why: Checks that the flowchart has the required input and output sequence.
rubric.description: Shows Start, input of two values, output of their sum, and Stop in the correct order.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct sequence with recognisable flowchart steps.

modelAnswer: (Oval) START
(Parallelogram) Input A, B
(Rectangle) SUM = A + B
(Parallelogram) Output SUM
(Oval) STOP

items.followUp: What is the difference between testing and debugging?

rubric.why: Checks the meaning of verification.
rubric.description: Verification checks whether the product is being built correctly according to specifications or requirements.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for distinguishing verification as checking conformance to specifications.

rubric.why: Checks the meaning of validation.
rubric.description: Validation checks whether the correct product is being built to meet user needs or intended use.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for distinguishing validation as checking user needs or intended use.

modelAnswer: Verification checks whether the product is being built correctly according to its specifications: “Are we building the product right?”
Validation checks whether the product meets users’ needs and intended use: “Are we building the right product?”
